originalTitle: A Developer's Guide to WebMCP: Shipping a 0% Adoption Standard
title: A Developer's Guide to WebMCP: Shipping a 0% Adoption Standard
oneSentenceSummary: A developer ships WebMCP on two sites despite 0% adoption across the top 200,000 domains, documenting the implementation, the null results, and the strategic case for being early on an emerging AI-web standard.
summary: This article presents a first-hand account of implementing WebMCP, a W3C Community Group Draft standard for enabling AI agents to call site tools directly, rather than just crawling HTML. The author scanned 111,076 of the top 200,000 websites and found zero production deployments of WebMCP. He then shipped it on two of his own sites: chudi.dev (using a SvelteKit polyfill) and citability.dev (using a .well-known manifest). The article details the full implementation code, the data on AI bot traffic and adoption curves for 17 emerging standards, and the honest result that after 93 days, zero AI agents have called his WebMCP tools. Despite the null result, the author argues that the low implementation cost, the compounding learning from a still-plastic spec, and the potential for early-mover dynamics when the adoption cliff moves make shipping now a worthwhile strategic bet. The piece includes practical step-by-step implementation guides for both SvelteKit and Next.js, and discusses the broader shift from passive permission signals (robots.txt) to active capability standards (WebMCP, A2A Agent Cards).

mainPoints.point: WebMCP has 0% adoption across the top 200,000 websites, but the author argues this is a starting point, not a ceiling.
mainPoints.explanation: A scan of 111,076 domains found zero production WebMCP deployments. The author shipped it anyway, arguing that the low implementation cost and potential early-mover advantage make it a worthwhile strategic bet.

mainPoints.point: The adoption curve for AI-web standards shows a cliff between passive signals and active capabilities.
mainPoints.explanation: Standards like robots.txt and ai.txt (passive permission signals) have high adoption, while standards like WebMCP and A2A Agent Cards (active capability descriptions) are near zero. This cliff represents an opportunity for early adopters.

mainPoints.point: The author's two implementations (polyfill and manifest) received zero agent calls, but this null result is the most informative part of the experiment.
mainPoints.explanation: After 93 days on chudi.dev and 5 days on citability.dev, no external AI agent invoked the WebMCP tools. This confirms the spec is pre-production, but the infrastructure is ready for when adoption begins.

mainPoints.point: Shipping early provides compounding learning from a still-plastic spec and positions sites for when the adoption cliff moves.
mainPoints.explanation: Implementing WebMCP reveals gaps and questions not apparent from reading the spec. When browser support arrives, early adopters will have working implementations and established infrastructure.

keyQuotes: I scanned 111,076 of the top 200,000 websites on the internet looking for a specific HTTP header. I found exactly zero.
The null result is the most informative part of this experiment.
The cost of being early is very low. The cost of being late is unclear but probably real.
The adoption curve starts somewhere. Right now, for WebMCP, that somewhere is you.
The cliff is not there because developers do not know about the active capability standards. It is there because those standards are not stable yet.

originalTitle: 面壁智能端侧双响开源：MiniCPM5-1B 以 1B 打败 2B，BitCPM-CANN 释放 6 倍显存红利
title: Face Intelligence Open-Sources Two Edge-Side Models: MiniCPM5-1B Beats 2B with 1B Parameters, BitCPM-CANN Unlocks 6x VRAM Efficiency
oneSentenceSummary: Face Intelligence, in collaboration with Tsinghua University, open-sources MiniCPM5-1B and BitCPM-CANN. The former surpasses 2B-level models with just 1B parameters, while the latter achieves 6x VRAM efficiency through 1.58-bit quantization, marking a breakthrough in domestic computing power based on the full Huawei Ascend stack.
summary: Face Intelligence, in partnership with Tsinghua University and the OpenBMB open-source community, released two models during the Edge-Side Large Model Open Source Week. MiniCPM5-1B, with only 1B parameters, surpasses all models under 2B parameters (including Qwen3.5-2B) on the AA-Index. After INT4 quantization, its weights are only 0.5GB, enabling it to run on mobile phones, browsers, and even pure CPU environments. Its training data employs a tiered data governance system, and it open-sources the high-quality synthetic dataset Ultra-FineWeb-L3. BitCPM-CANN is a 1.58-bit ternary large model fully trained end-to-end on the Huawei Ascend platform, available in four sizes: 0.5B, 1B, 3B, and 8B. Compared to BF16, it unlocks approximately 6x VRAM efficiency while retaining 90%-97.2% of its capabilities. The article also details model deployment and fine-tuning methods, highlighting that the ForgeTrain framework was entirely written by AI, validating the feasibility of AI manufacturing AI.

mainPoints.point: MiniCPM5-1B surpasses all models under 2B parameters on the AA-Index with just 1B parameters, setting a new record for intelligence density.
mainPoints.explanation: Through tiered data governance and high-quality synthetic data, this model demonstrates that small models can achieve higher intelligence density with careful training, validating the Density Law that intelligence density doubles every 3.5 months.

mainPoints.point: BitCPM-CANN adopts 1.58-bit quantization-aware training, unlocking approximately 6x VRAM efficiency while retaining over 90% of its capabilities.
mainPoints.explanation: Unlike post-training quantization, BitCPM-CANN learns to represent knowledge with ternary weights from the initial training stage, fundamentally improving information density. This allows an 8B model to run smoothly on flagship smartphones.

mainPoints.point: BitCPM-CANN is fully trained end-to-end on the Huawei Ascend platform, overcoming the challenge of extreme low-bit training on domestic computing power.
mainPoints.explanation: From quantization operators to the training framework, the entire pipeline is natively completed on Ascend, filling the gap in low-bit model supply for domestic NPUs. It proves that Ascend can not only train large models but also achieve world-class extreme low-bit training.

mainPoints.point: The ForgeTrain training framework was entirely written by AI, validating the recursive self-improvement path of AI manufacturing AI.
mainPoints.explanation: ForgeTrain's training speed on H100 surpasses NVIDIA's Megatron framework by 10%. Its success demonstrates the feasibility of AI autonomously writing production-grade code and achieving leading results.

keyQuotes: MiniCPM5-1B once again pushes the upper limit of model intelligence density: with only 1B parameters, it surpasses all models under 2B parameters on the AA-Index.

BitCPM-CANN adopts the quantization-aware training (QAT) approach... allowing the model to 'grow natively' under the constraints of extremely low bit-width, forcing every bit to maximize information density and knowledge carrying efficiency.
This is the first publicly available result on the Ascend platform to complete end-to-end 1.58-bit training and conduct full-precision comparative evaluations.
It's not about waiting for hardware to become stronger to adapt to the model, but about making the model smarter to adapt to the hardware.

originalTitle: Slack AI: The Path to Multi-Cloud
title: Slack AI: The Path to Multi-Cloud
oneSentenceSummary: Slack Engineering details its multi-year journey from AWS SageMaker to a multi-cloud AI architecture on AWS Bedrock and GCP Vertex AI, driven by the need for operational efficiency, model agility, and enterprise-grade reliability.
summary: This article chronicles Slack AI's architectural evolution over three years, moving through four distinct phases to achieve a multi-cloud, multi-model AI serving platform. Starting with AWS SageMaker, the team faced operational overhead and model feature lag. They migrated to Amazon Bedrock for managed simplicity and immediate model access, but encountered efficiency gaps with Provisioned Throughput. This led to a hybrid strategy combining Provisioned and On-Demand capacity, and the development of an intelligent routing layer with model hierarchies and circuit breakers. The final phase expanded to Google Cloud's Vertex AI, creating a true multi-cloud footprint for infrastructural redundancy, model-to-feature optimization, and access to innovation. The article details the technical challenges, trade-offs, and engineering solutions at each stage, emphasizing the importance of abstraction layers, gradual migration, and cross-functional alignment.

mainPoints.point: Slack's AI infrastructure evolved from self-managed SageMaker to a multi-cloud architecture for better efficiency and model access.
mainPoints.explanation: The journey moved through four phases: SageMaker, Bedrock Provisioned Throughput, Bedrock On-Demand, and finally a multi-cloud strategy with GCP Vertex AI, each solving specific operational and agility challenges.

mainPoints.point: A hybrid strategy using both Provisioned and On-Demand capacity optimizes cost and performance for variable workloads.
mainPoints.explanation: High-volume, latency-sensitive features use dedicated Provisioned Throughput, while bursty workloads use On-Demand. A spillover pattern ensures no requests are dropped during surges.

mainPoints.point: An intelligent routing layer with circuit breakers and model hierarchies is critical for multi-cloud resilience.
mainPoints.explanation: This layer uses real-time metrics to select the best model/provider, automatically reroutes traffic during degradation, and enables seamless A/B testing of new models.

mainPoints.point: Multi-cloud architecture provides redundancy, model-to-feature optimization, and access to vendor-exclusive innovations.
mainPoints.explanation: By expanding to GCP, Slack eliminated single points of failure, achieved a 10% quality improvement and 67% latency reduction for specific tasks, and gained strategic flexibility.

keyQuotes: We didn't just want shiny new models; we needed a system resilient to regional outages and GPU scarcity.
The most critical decision wasn't which model to use, but how we built the logic around them.
An LLM service that is 'up' but slow is effectively broken.
The future of enterprise AI is multi-cloud, multi-model, and dynamically orchestrated.
Measure first, migrate gradually, and monitor continuously.

originalTitle: From TF-IDF to Transformers: Implementing Four Generations of Semantic Search
title: From TF-IDF to Transformers: Implementing Four Generations of Semantic Search
oneSentenceSummary: This article traces the evolution of semantic search through four implemented methods, from TF-IDF with handcrafted rules to fine-tuned transformer models, using a concrete example of comparing art critiques.
summary: The article provides a hands-on, educational walkthrough of four generations of semantic search systems, using the task of comparing a student's art critique with expert critiques as a consistent example. It begins with a rule-based system combining TF-IDF cosine similarity with heuristic features like keyword overlap and recency. The second method replaces handcrafted rules with supervised learning, using Logistic Regression on TF-IDF features to classify critiques as expert-like or novice-like. The third method introduces dense semantic embeddings from a Sentence Transformer, enabling similarity comparisons based on meaning rather than exact vocabulary. The final method fine-tunes a DistilBERT transformer model for contextual classification. The article discusses the strengths and limitations of each approach, emphasizing the trade-off between interpretability and semantic understanding, and highlights the progression from human-designed features to learned representations.

mainPoints.point: Semantic search evolved from keyword matching to contextual language understanding through four distinct methodological stages.
mainPoints.explanation: The article demonstrates a clear progression: from TF-IDF with handcrafted rules, to classical ML on TF-IDF features, to embedding-based semantic similarity, and finally to fine-tuned transformer models.

mainPoints.point: TF-IDF with rule-based scoring is highly interpretable but limited by its reliance on exact vocabulary overlap.
mainPoints.explanation: The first method's ranking is transparent and understandable, but it fails to capture semantic similarity when different words express similar ideas, motivating the need for more advanced techniques.

mainPoints.point: Supervised learning on TF-IDF features shifts from manual rule design to data-driven pattern learning, but still lacks true semantic understanding.
mainPoints.explanation: Logistic Regression learns which words correlate with expert writing, offering interpretability through feature coefficients, but it cannot grasp context or meaning beyond word frequencies.

mainPoints.point: Embedding-based methods using Sentence Transformers enable semantic similarity comparisons independent of exact wording.
mainPoints.explanation: By representing text as dense vectors in a semantic space, critiques discussing similar artistic ideas can be recognized as similar even when using different vocabulary, marking a major advance.

mainPoints.point: Fine-tuned transformer models provide the deepest contextual understanding but require large datasets and risk overfitting.
mainPoints.explanation: Fine-tuning DistilBERT allows the model to analyze relationships between words and sentence structure, but with small datasets, it may memorize patterns rather than generalize, as shown by the example of a critique classified differently after 30 vs. 100 epochs.

keyQuotes: The history of semantic search is also the story of an important shift in AI itself: from transparent, human-designed systems to increasingly intelligent models whose internal reasoning is much more difficult to interpret.
The method primarily captures surface-level vocabulary patterns rather than deeper semantic meaning.
This is an important shift because the system now learns from data rather than relying on hand-crafted rules.
Two critiques can use very different language to describe an artistic idea, and yet they are still recognized as similar.
Transformers usually require large amounts of training data.

originalTitle: 近 9 倍训练加速：DiT 里的残差流，正在成为收敛瓶颈
title: Nearly 9x Training Acceleration: Residual Stream in DiT Becomes a Convergence Bottleneck
oneSentenceSummary: Nanjing University and Alibaba jointly propose Diffusion-Adaptive Routing (DAR), which replaces the fixed residual summation in DiT with a learnable, time-dynamic cross-layer routing mechanism, achieving nearly 9x training acceleration and improved generation quality.
summary: This paper, a collaboration between the LAMDA Lab at Nanjing University and the Alibaba Intelligent Engine Team, systematically analyzes the limitations of standard residual connections in Diffusion Transformers (DiT) within the context of diffusion models. The study finds that fixed-weight residual summation leads to hidden state explosion in deeper layers, gradient attenuation, and inter-layer redundancy, while failing to adapt to the varying information needs of different denoising stages. To address this, the paper proposes Diffusion-Adaptive Routing (DAR), which reframes the residual stream as a learnable, time-dynamic cross-layer information routing mechanism. DAR allows each layer to selectively aggregate information from the outputs of previous layers via softmax routing and introduces timestep awareness, enabling routing weights to adapt dynamically based on the noise stage. To control memory overhead, DAR adopts a chunked aggregation strategy, balancing historical information retention with computational efficiency. On ImageNet 256x256, DAR reduces the FID of SiT-XL/2 from 9.67 to 7.56 and achieves baseline convergence quality with approximately 8.75x fewer training iterations. When combined with REPA, it yields about 2x acceleration in the early training phase. Additionally, DAR demonstrates the ability to preserve high-frequency details in the post-training and distillation of Qwen-Image. This work redefines the residual stream from a default engineering detail to an architectural variable worthy of systematic study.

mainPoints.point: Standard residual connections become a convergence bottleneck in DiT, causing deep state explosion, gradient attenuation, and inter-layer redundancy.
mainPoints.explanation: Fixed-weight residual summation causes hidden state magnitudes to grow nearly 100x along the network depth, leads to rapid gradient decay in backpropagation, and results in adjacent block output similarities consistently above 0.9, limiting model expressiveness and training efficiency.

mainPoints.point: DAR replaces fixed residual summation with a learnable, time-dynamic softmax routing mechanism, allowing each layer to select its information source based on the denoising stage.
mainPoints.explanation: By using query-key scoring and softmax aggregation of historical layer outputs, and incorporating timestep embeddings to make routing weights adapt dynamically to the noise stage, DAR solves the problem of fixed summation failing to meet the information needs of different denoising phases.

mainPoints.point: DAR achieves 8.75x training acceleration on ImageNet 256x256, reducing FID from 9.67 to 7.56, and is orthogonal to REPA.
mainPoints.explanation: Experiments show DAR improves FID by 2.11 under ODE sampling and achieves 6.92 under SDE; when combined with REPA, it reaches an FID of 7.09 at 100K iterations, surpassing the result of REPA alone at 200K, demonstrating the complementary nature of their optimization directions.

mainPoints.point: The chunked aggregation strategy balances historical information retention with memory overhead, with an optimal chunk size of approximately 4.
mainPoints.explanation: Through rate-distortion analysis, the optimal chunk size is theoretically predicted to be between 3.7 and 4.9, consistent with the best-performing c4 in experiments, avoiding the memory explosion of dense routing and the information loss from excessive compression.

keyQuotes: Information aggregation in DiT should no longer remain a fixed, incremental residual summation; it should be designed as a learnable, time-dynamic, non-incremental routing mechanism.

DAR views the residual stream as an information aggregation process along the depth dimension. Instead of directly summing the outputs of previous layers, it allows the current layer to perform a softmax routing over historical outputs to determine which sources are more valuable.
The benefit of DAR is not simply increasing connection density, but enabling the connection pattern to adapt dynamically with depth and timestep.

Model performance depends not only on how each layer computes internally, but also on how information flows between layers. The residual stream is not a default choice; it is a part of the generative model architecture that can be learned, tuned, and is worth redesigning.

originalTitle: Safer Than YOLO: Auto Mode for Exec Approvals
title: Safer Than YOLO: Auto Mode for Exec Approvals
oneSentenceSummary: OpenClaw introduces an opt-in 'auto' mode for host exec approvals that uses a reviewer model to handle low-risk policy misses, reducing prompt noise while keeping human fallback for uncertain commands.
summary: OpenClaw Blog announces a new 'auto' mode for host exec approvals, designed to be a safer middle ground between the strict 'humanfirst' mode and the permissive 'YOLO' mode. In 'auto' mode, commands that match an allowlist or safe-bin rule run automatically. Commands that miss policy are first sent to a separate reviewer model (configurable, e.g., a frontier model like GPT-5.5) for a low-risk, one-time execution decision. If the reviewer is uncertain, the command times out, or is high-risk, it falls back to a human operator. This pattern mirrors OpenAI's Guardian system in Codex. The article details the workflow, configuration steps, security considerations, and the routing of approval prompts to channels like Slack and Telegram. The key principle is to protect users without removing operator choice, making it ideal for enterprise environments that need a balance of speed and safety.

mainPoints.point: OpenClaw introduces 'auto' mode as a safer alternative to 'YOLO' for host exec approvals.
mainPoints.explanation: Auto mode uses a reviewer model to handle low-risk policy misses, reducing approval prompts while maintaining a human fallback for uncertain or high-risk commands, offering a balance between speed and safety.

mainPoints.point: The reviewer model is separate from the main agent model, allowing for flexible configuration.
mainPoints.explanation: Users can keep a local model for the main agent and use a more powerful frontier model (e.g., GPT-5.5) specifically for reviewing host exec requests, optimizing for both cost and judgment quality.

mainPoints.point: The 'auto' mode workflow is deterministic and layered, ensuring safety without excessive friction.
mainPoints.explanation: Commands first check an allowlist, then a deterministic safe-bin rule. If they miss, a bounded review packet is sent to the reviewer. Only low-risk, one-time executions can be auto-approved; everything else falls back to a human.

mainPoints.point: Approval prompts can be routed to communication channels like Slack and Telegram.
mainPoints.explanation: This moves approvals out of the terminal and into places operators already monitor, improving workflow integration and response times for enterprise teams.

keyQuotes: Auto is the mode that fits Enterprise environments best: policy runs first, low-risk misses can be reviewed by a model, and anything uncertain still routes to a human.

The reviewer model is separate from the main agent model. You can keep the agent on local models for normal work and point exec review at a frontier model such as `openai/gpt-5.5` when you want stronger judgment on approval misses.
`auto` does not override local safety settings. A host configured to always ask still asks. A host configured to deny still denies.
We are not changing the default today. `auto` is an opt-in path we are testing in public.

originalTitle: Welcome NVIDIA Cosmos 3: The First Open Omni-model for Physical AI Reasoning and Action
title: Welcome NVIDIA Cosmos 3: The First Open Omni-model for Physical AI Reasoning and Action
oneSentenceSummary: NVIDIA releases Cosmos 3, the first open omni-model for physical AI that unifies world generation, physical reasoning, and action generation into a single Mixture-of-Transformers architecture.
summary: NVIDIA has released Cosmos 3, a major advancement in world foundation models for physical AI. Unlike previous versions that required separate models for world generation, reasoning, and policy generation, Cosmos 3 is a unified omni-model built on a Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) architecture. It processes text, image, video, audio, and action modalities within a single framework, using an autoregressive subsequence for reasoning and a diffusion subsequence for generation, connected via joint attention. The release includes two model sizes: Cosmos 3 Nano (8B parameters) for workstation-grade GPUs and Cosmos 3 Super (32B parameters) for large-scale synthetic data generation and research. Cosmos 3 is available on Hugging Face with Diffusers integration, post-training scripts on GitHub, and a set of open synthetic data generation datasets for robotics, autonomous driving, and warehouse safety. The model supports multiple input-output modality combinations including text/image/video to video, video to text/action, and image/text to video and action, making it suitable for applications like robot policy learning, autonomous driving simulation, and synthetic training data generation.

mainPoints.point: Cosmos 3 is the first open omni-model for physical AI, unifying world generation, reasoning, and action generation.
mainPoints.explanation: Previous Cosmos releases required separate models for different capabilities. Cosmos 3 combines all of them into a single model with a Mixture-of-Transformers architecture, enabling seamless switching between VLM, video generation, forward/inverse dynamics, and robot policy tasks.

mainPoints.point: The architecture uses joint attention between autoregressive and diffusion subsequences within each transformer layer.
mainPoints.explanation: Input sequences are split into an AR subsequence for reasoning via next-token prediction and a DM subsequence for generation via iterative denoising. They share joint attention, allowing a single model to handle both reasoning and generation without architectural changes.

mainPoints.point: Two model sizes are available: Cosmos 3 Nano (8B) for workstation GPUs and Cosmos 3 Super (32B) for large-scale research.
mainPoints.explanation: The Nano variant runs on RTX PRO 6000-class hardware, while the Super variant targets NVIDIA Hopper and Blackwell GPUs for synthetic data generation at scale. Both are available on Hugging Face with Diffusers integration.

mainPoints.point: NVIDIA is releasing open synthetic data generation datasets for physical AI domains.
mainPoints.explanation: The SDG datasets cover robotics simulation, physics simulation, spatial reasoning, human motion, autonomous driving, and warehouse safety, providing training and evaluation data for the physical AI community.

keyQuotes: Cosmos 3 represents a major leap forward in world foundation models (WFMs) for physical AI: a single, unified omni-model that combines world generation, physical reasoning, and action generation in one model.

AR and DM tokens use separate parameter sets within each transformer layer but interact through joint attention - this is what lets a single model seamlessly switch between acting as a VLM, a video generator, a forward/inverse dynamics model, or a robot policy without any architectural changes.
Cosmos 3 helps build physical AI systems capable of understanding the real world. Not just pixels and tokens, but motion, causality, physics, and action.

originalTitle: Beyond the Menu Tree: How Yelp Built a Smarter Customer Success Chatbot with AI
title: Beyond the Menu Tree: How Yelp Built a Smarter Customer Success Chatbot with AI
oneSentenceSummary: Yelp's engineering team details how they built a smarter customer success chatbot by replacing a rigid menu-tree system with a RAG pipeline that uses only article metadata for efficient retrieval, achieving a 94% recall@5 and doubling the resolution rate.
summary: This article from the Yelp Engineering Blog describes the evolution of their Customer Success chatbot from a static, rule-based system to a dynamic, LLM-powered conversational agent. The core innovation is a Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) pipeline that intelligently routes user queries into specialized workflows (QA, Billing, Refund, etc.). For the primary QA workflow, the team built a lean and highly accurate vectorstore by embedding only the metadata (title, summary, headers) from their ~370 Support Center articles, rather than the full article text. This approach, using OpenAI's text-embedding-ada-002 and FAISS for search, resulted in a compact 8MB in-memory index with a 94% recall@5. The article also covers their daily update pipeline for fresh knowledge, a solution for mitigating LLM hallucination of hyperlinks, and future plans for improvement. The project resulted in a doubling of the chatbot's resolution rate.

mainPoints.point: Yelp replaced a rigid menu-tree chatbot with an LLM-powered system using a RAG pipeline.
mainPoints.explanation: The legacy system relied on fixed phrases and a 2-step menu, failing when queries didn't match exactly. The new system uses an LLM to route queries into specialized workflows and a RAG pipeline to ground answers in the company's knowledge base.

mainPoints.point: The RAG pipeline achieves high accuracy by embedding only article metadata, not full text.
mainPoints.explanation: To avoid diluting the semantic signal, the team embedded only the title, summary, and top headers from each Support Center article as separate vectors. This created a compact 8MB index that enables fast and precise retrieval.

mainPoints.point: The system achieved a 94% recall@5 on its evaluation dataset.
mainPoints.explanation: By using FAISS for indexing and a multi-step retrieval process (finding top-k matches, applying a similarity threshold, and selecting the top 5 unique articles), the system reliably finds the most relevant articles for the LLM's context.

mainPoints.point: A dedicated solution was built to prevent LLM hallucination of hyperlinks.
mainPoints.explanation: The LLM frequently invented URLs. Yelp solved this by implementing a validation check that ensures any link in the final response originates from a retrieved Support Center article, guaranteeing accuracy.

keyQuotes: We discovered that embedding large texts, such as entire articles or long paragraphs, can dilute the information signal, often leading to less accurate semantic matching.
By focusing on concise metadata, we ensure maximum semantic similarity capture during the search phase.
This retrieval methodology achieves robust results, demonstrating an impressive ~94% recall@5 on our evaluation dataset.
The transition from the legacy chatbot to our LLM-Assisted CS Chatbot...represents a significant milestone for Yelp Customer Success.

originalTitle: AI Infra 入门干货总结：大模型是如何高效推理的
title: A Practical Guide to AI Infra: How Large Models Perform Efficient Inference
oneSentenceSummary: Based on an in-depth reading of the vLLM source code, this article uses Llama 3 as an example to systematically explain the complete efficient inference pipeline of large models, from Tokenize to Sampling, by tracing the tensor dimension changes at each step.
summary: This article summarizes the author's two months of spare-time deep dive into the vLLM source code. Focusing on Decoder-Only LLMs, and using Llama 3 as an example, it breaks down the complete inference pipeline from Tokenize, Embedding Lookup, Transformer Block (Attention and FFN) to LM Head and Sampling. The core highlight is that the author annotates the tensor dimension changes at each computational step and provides an in-depth explanation of how two key technologies, Continuous Batching and Paged Attention, improve inference efficiency. The article also explores the fundamental differences between the Prefill and Decode phases in terms of computation and memory access, and how FlashAttention breaks the memory wall through Online Softmax. Finally, it concludes that the MLP layer is compute-bound while the Attention layer is memory-bound, and includes a table of model configuration parameters and runtime variables, offering a solid introductory reference for AI Infra practitioners.

mainPoints.point: Continuous Batching shifts the scheduling granularity from the request level down to the token level, significantly boosting GPU utilization.
mainPoints.explanation: By scheduling at the token level, multiple requests can reuse model weights, transforming operations like QKV_Proj, O_Proj, and MLP from matrix-vector multiplications (GEMV) back into matrix multiplications (GEMM), thus amortizing the memory cost of loading weights.

mainPoints.point: Paged Attention manages KV Cache using a virtual page table mechanism, solving the memory fragmentation problem.
mainPoints.explanation: Similar to virtual memory in operating systems, Paged Attention allocates non-contiguous physical blocks for each request and uses a block table for indirect addressing, greatly improving GPU memory utilization. This is the foundation for supporting high-performance inference with Continuous Batching.

mainPoints.point: The Prefill phase is compute-bound, while the Decode phase is memory-bound.
mainPoints.explanation: The Prefill phase processes a large number of tokens, has high computational intensity, and is limited by Tensor Cores compute power. The Decode phase processes only one token at a time, requiring the transfer of a large amount of KV Cache and model weights from HBM, and is therefore limited by memory bandwidth.

mainPoints.point: FlashAttention breaks the memory wall through kernel fusion and the Online Softmax algorithm.
mainPoints.explanation: FlashAttention fuses Q-K dot product, Softmax, and multiplication by V into a single CUDA kernel, computing in blocks within SRAM. This avoids writing large intermediate matrices to HBM, significantly improving the performance of Attention computation.

keyQuotes: What if we could shift the scheduling granularity from the request level down to the token level? Congratulations, you've just invented continuous batching.

Should the KV Cache memory allocation for each request also be at the token level, instead of allocating all memory at once? What if we use an address array (block table) to manage the KV Cache addresses for each request? Congratulations, you've just invented Paged Attention.

Compared to OOM caused by memory fragmentation, sacrificing a small amount of memory bandwidth for a significant increase in overall system throughput is a worthwhile trade-off in the overall logic of LLM inference.
Don't rebuild from scratch; instead, learn the 'correction value' (Delta) based on the original. This is the physical foundation of the 'Scaling Law' in architecture.

From an inference perspective alone, the principles of large models are actually not that esoteric. The most difficult mathematical formula is probably RoPE. But there is so much to learn in AI Infra... It's endless.

originalTitle: Skill 文档也能训练？SkillOpt：把 Agent 的经验写进一份可优化说明书
title: Can Skill Documents Be Trained? SkillOpt: Turning Agent Experience into an Optimizable Manual
oneSentenceSummary: This article interprets Microsoft's paper SkillOpt, which proposes treating an Agent's Skill documents as trainable external states, enabling automated iterative optimization through mechanisms like rollout, reflection, bounded edits, and validation gates.
summary: This article provides a detailed interpretation of Microsoft's paper SkillOpt, which introduces a method for optimizing an Agent's Skill documents (i.e., prompts, manuals, or workflow specifications) as trainable external states. The article points out that traditional Skill documents are either written manually or generated by LLMs in a single pass, lacking a feedback loop. SkillOpt, in contrast, mimics the deep learning training paradigm by treating Skill documents as parameters and iteratively optimizing them in text space through mechanisms such as rollout (executing tasks), reflection (analyzing trajectories), bounded edits (constrained modifications), validation gates (verification), and rejected-edit buffers (negative feedback). Experimental results show that SkillOpt achieves optimal or tied-optimal performance across all 52 evaluation items, with significant improvements over baselines without Skills on multiple benchmarks, especially on tool-based tasks like Spreadsheet. The article also analyzes ablation study results for core components of SkillOpt (such as learning rate, rejected buffer, and slow update) and provides simplified recommendations for real-world implementation.

mainPoints.point: SkillOpt treats an Agent's Skill documents as trainable external states rather than static prompts.
mainPoints.explanation: The paper proposes that Skill documents should be repeatedly trained, validated, and iterated upon based on task feedback, much like model weights, to continuously improve the stability of Agent execution.

mainPoints.point: SkillOpt mimics the deep learning training paradigm, implementing a complete optimization pipeline in text space.
mainPoints.explanation: By leveraging mechanisms such as rollout (forward propagation), reflection (backward propagation), bounded edits (gradient updates), validation gates (verification), and rejected-edit buffers (negative feedback), a closed-loop Skill optimizer is constructed.

mainPoints.point: Experimental results show that SkillOpt achieves significant performance gains on multiple benchmarks, especially on tool-based tasks.
mainPoints.explanation: Achieving optimal or tied-optimal performance across all 52 evaluation items, with improvements of over 50 percentage points on tasks like Spreadsheet, demonstrates the method's effectiveness in operational tasks.

originalTitle: TogetherAI 开源 OSCAR：超越 TurboQuant! 面向真实 Serving 的 2-bit KV Cache 量化
title: TogetherAI Open Sources OSCAR: Surpassing TurboQuant! 2-bit KV Cache Quantization for Real-World Serving
oneSentenceSummary: Together AI has open-sourced OSCAR, a 2-bit KV Cache quantization scheme designed for real-world long-context serving. By employing attention-aware rotation techniques, it significantly reduces memory footprint and boosts inference throughput while maintaining model performance comparable to BF16 precision.
summary: This article details Together AI's open-source OSCAR (Offline Spectral Covariance-Aware Rotation) scheme, which aims to solve the KV Cache memory bottleneck in long-context LLM inference. OSCAR's core innovation lies not in simply reconstructing the K/V vectors with low error, but in analyzing the attention mechanism to push quantization noise into directions that are insensitive to attention. Specifically, OSCAR uses query covariance to guide key rotation and score-weighted value covariance to guide value rotation, combined with Hadamard transform and bit-reversal techniques, achieving efficient quantization at approximately 2.28 effective bits per KV element. On the system implementation side, OSCAR has been integrated into SGLang, managing KV Cache with a three-stage token pool (BF16 sink + INT2 history + BF16 recent), and is compatible with paged KV and prefix cache. Evaluation results show that on models like Qwen3 and GLM-4.7, OSCAR's performance at 2-bit precision is close to BF16, improving by up to 40.1 points over 3-bit TurboQuant, achieving up to ~3x decode speedup and up to ~7x job-level throughput improvement. The article also provides a quick practical guide for deploying OSCAR on SGLang.

mainPoints.point: OSCAR uses attention-aware rotation techniques to steer quantization noise towards directions insensitive to attention.
mainPoints.explanation: Unlike traditional methods that aim for low reconstruction error of K/V vectors, OSCAR uses query covariance and score-weighted value covariance to guide the generation of rotation matrices, ensuring that the quantized KV Cache has minimal impact on attention computation.

mainPoints.point: OSCAR achieves performance close to BF16 at approximately 2.28 BPE, significantly outperforming other 2-bit and 3-bit schemes.
mainPoints.explanation: On models like Qwen3-8B, OSCAR shows minimal performance gap compared to BF16 on tasks such as GPQA and HumanEval, and significantly outperforms QuaRot-INT2 and TurboQuant, demonstrating its ability to maintain model quality under high compression rates.

mainPoints.point: OSCAR is integrated into SGLang with a three-stage token pool design, balancing precision and efficiency.
mainPoints.explanation: During runtime, the KV Cache is divided into three segments: BF16 sink, INT2 history, and BF16 recent. This protects the precision of attention sinks and recent context while drastically compressing the memory footprint of historical KV, and is compatible with paged KV and prefix cache.

mainPoints.point: OSCAR delivers significant memory savings and inference acceleration in long-context scenarios.
mainPoints.explanation: Compared to BF16, OSCAR can reduce KV Cache memory by approximately 8x, achieving up to ~3x decode speedup and ~7x job-level throughput improvement under 100k context, making it particularly suitable for Agent scenarios with long prefix reuse.

keyQuotes: OSCAR's core idea is: don't just aim to reconstruct the K/V vectors themselves, but to preserve the way attention truly consumes these KV values.
OSCAR's advantage is not just making the numerical distribution smoother, but pushing quantization noise into directions that are relatively insensitive to attention.
OSCAR doesn't simply 'add a rotation'; it incorporates rotation, clipping, and grouping into the objective function of attention quality.
OSCAR is designed for deployable enterprise workloads, not just to show the paper's bleak error data.

The key insight from OSCAR is: for 2-bit KV Cache to truly go online, rotation must not only 'exist' but be aligned with attention; simultaneously, it must be designed together within a real serving system.
